Action Plan:
1. Prescribe spacer device; pharmacist to demonstrate correct inhaler-with-spacer technique at collection.  
2. Advise increased salbutamol (short-acting β2-agonist) use: 2–4 puffs via spacer every 4 hours as needed until symptoms settle.  
3. Prescribe peak-flow meter; instruct patient to record readings on waking and in the evening for the next week.  
4. Initiate regular oral antihistamine (OTC, daily) for concurrent hay-fever control; medication name and dose to be selected by patient/pharmacist.  
5. Safety-netting: if temperature rises, wheeze/shortness of breath worsens, or peak-flow falls markedly, patient to telephone clinic urgently.  
6. Arrange telephone/virtual asthma review in 1 week (or sooner if deterioration) to assess symptom course and review peak-flow diary; consider stepping-up controller therapy at that visit.  
7. Advise continuing work from home/sick leave until exercise tolerance returns; may resume walking to work once dyspnoea resolves.  
8. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint: Wheeze and shortness of breath for 2–3 days; associated dry cough, self-reported “fever” (measured 37 °C).  
• Exertional limitation: unable to walk to work, occasional difficulty finishing sentences; symptoms improve at rest.  
• No chest pain, haemoptysis, or nocturnal symptoms; no phlegm production.  

Past Medical History  
• Asthma since childhood, previously severe enough for occasional hospital visits; largely quiescent but uses salbutamol inhaler intermittently.  
• Hay fever.  
• Eczema.  

Medications  
• Salbutamol inhaler, dose/route/frequency not documented (patient estimates every few weeks and before exercise).  
• No other regular medications.

Social History  
• 33-year-old engineer; lives with partner.  
• Non-smoker.  
• Alcohol: ~1 glass of wine every 2–3 days.  

Allergies  
• No known drug allergies.  

Objective:
• Remote consultation—no in-person exam.  
• Patient-reported temperature: 37 °C (normal).  
• No other vitals or physical findings documented.  
• No investigations performed to date.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Issue: Acute wheeze / dyspnoea  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation (DDx item: “Acute asthma exacerbation” – High likelihood).  
   - Differential diagnosis:  
     • Viral respiratory tract infection / acute bronchitis with reactive airway (Medium).  
     • Allergic (pollen-induced) asthma flare (Medium).  
     • Pulmonary embolism (Low).  
     • Community-acquired pneumonia (Low).  
   - Investigations planned: Peak-flow diary for one week; consider further tests if poor response or atypical course.  
   - Treatment planned: Increase salbutamol frequency (2–4 puffs q4h PRN), prescribe spacer, start regular antihistamine, provide safety-net advice.  
   - Referrals: None immediately; routine asthma review with primary-care clinician in one week.

Quality checks:
• Missing elements: objective vitals (pulse, respiratory rate, SpO₂, BP), full medication list reconciliation, patient’s full demographic details, inhaler technique check, allergy confirmation for non-drug allergens.  
• No internal conflicts between transcript and DDx identified.  
• Transcript quality: Clear overall; occasional minor inaudible words but clinical meaning preserved.
